# Lecture 14.2: Product Measure

## Product $\sigma$-Algebras and Projections

Let $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2)$ be measurable spaces.

::: {#def-product-sigma-algebra}
The **product $\sigma$-algebra**, denoted $\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$, is the $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2$ generated by product sets (rectangles) $A_1 \times A_2$ with $A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1$ and $A_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2$:
$$
\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2 \triangleq \sigma(\{ A_1 \times A_2 \mid A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1, A_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2 \})
$$ {#eq-product-sigma-def}

More generally, for a finite family of measurable spaces $\{(\Omega_j, \mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j=1}^d$:
$$
\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j \triangleq \sigma\left( \left\{ \prod_{j=1}^d B_j \;\middle|\; B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \text{ for } 1 \le j \le d \right\} \right)
$$ {#eq-d-product-sigma}
:::

* **Canonical Projections:** For an arbitrary index set $J$ and measurable spaces $\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}$, let $\pi_k: \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j \to \Omega_k$ be the coordinate map $\pi_k\big((\omega_j)_{j \in J}\big) = \omega_k$. When $J = \{1,\dots,d\}$ we write $\pi_k(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_d) = \omega_k$.

:::{#exm-product-space-coordinate}
## Two-dimensional product space
Let $\Omega=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ and consider the first and second coordinate maps $\pi_1(x,y)=x$ and $\pi_2(x,y)=y$. Take $A=(0,1]$. Then
$$ 
\pi_1^{-1}(A) = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x\in(0,1]\}. 
$$
Equivalently, $\pi_1^{-1}((0,1]) = (0,1]\times\mathbb R$. Geometrically, this is a vertical strip in $\mathbb R^2$.

Take $B=[2,5]$. Under the second coordinate projection, we have
$$ 
\pi_2^{-1}([2,5]) = \{(x,y):y\in[2,5]\}. 
$$
Therefore, $\pi_2^{-1}([2,5])=\mathbb{R}\times[2,5]$.

Finally, note that the intersection of cylinder sets is again a cylinder set. For example,
$$
\pi_1^{-1}((0,1]) \cap \pi_2^{-1}([2,5]) = (0,1] \times [2,5],
$$
which restricts both the first and second coordinates.
:::


Definition @def-product-sigma-algebra covers only **finite** families. For an arbitrary index set the correct notion is generated by *cylinders*, not by unrestricted products; see @rem-uncountable-products below.

:::{#def-cylinders}
## Cylinder Sets
A **cylinder set** in the product $\Omega = \prod_{j\in J}\Omega_j$ is a set of the form $\prod_{j\in J}B_j$ with $B_j\in\mathcal F_j$ for every $j\in J$ and $B_j=\Omega_j$ for all but finitely many $j$. In particular, a cylinder that restricts only the $j$-th coordinate is of the form $\pi_j^{-1}(B_j)=\prod_{k\in J}B_k$, where
$$
B_k=
\begin{cases}
B_j,&k=j,\\
\Omega_k,&k\neq j.
\end{cases}
$$
:::

- For a product space $\Omega=S_1\times\cdots\times S_N$, the inverse image of a set under the $n$th coordinate map has the form
$$
\pi_n^{-1}(A) = S_1\times\cdots\times S_{n-1} \times A\times S_{n+1}\times\cdots\times S_N.
$$
This is called a cylinder set: we restrict one coordinate and leave all the other coordinates unrestricted.



:::{#exm-cylinder}
## A cylinder set in $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$
Consider the product space $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}} = \{(x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots):x_j\in\mathbb R\}$. Define
$$ 
C = [0,1]\times[2,3]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots. 
$$
This is a cylinder set because $B_1=[0,1]$, $B_2=[2,3]$, and $B_j=\mathbb R\quad(j\ge3)$, so only finitely many coordinates are restricted. Equivalently,
$$ 
C = \left\{ x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}: x_1\in[0,1],\ x_2\in[2,3] \right\}. 
$$
In terms of coordinate projections, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_1^{-1}([0,1])=\{ x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}: x_1\in[0,1] \} = [0,1]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots,\\
&\pi_2^{-1}([2,3])=\{ x\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}: x_2\in[2,3] \}= \mathbb R\times[2,3]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots.
\end{aligned}
$$
Then,
$$ 
\begin{aligned}
C &= [0,1]\times[2,3]\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\cdots\\
&= \pi_1^{-1}([0,1]) \cap \pi_2^{-1}([2,3]).
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

:::{#exm-cylinder-coin-tosses}
## Cylinder events for an infinite sequence of coin tosses
Consider the sample space $\Omega=\{H,T\}^{\mathbb N}$, where an element $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\ldots)$ represents an infinite sequence of coin tosses. Define the cylinder set
$$ 
C=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_1=H,\ \omega_3=T,\ \omega_7=H\}. 
$$
In product notation,
$$ 
\begin{aligned}
C &= \{H\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{T\} \times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\\
&\times\{H\} \times\prod_{j=8}^{\infty}\{H,T\}. 
\end{aligned}
$$
This is a cylinder set because only three coordinates are restricted: 1, 3, and 7. All other coordinates are unrestricted. Equivalently, if $\pi_j(\omega)=\omega_j$ denotes the $j$-th coordinate projection, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_1^{-1}(\{H\})=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_1=H\} = \{H\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\cdots\\
&\pi_3^{-1}(\{T\})=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_3=T\} = \{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\cdots\\
&\pi_7^{-1}(\{H\})=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_7=H\} = \{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\\
&\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H,T\}\times\{H\}\times\cdots
\end{aligned}
$$
Then, we can express $C$ as the intersection of these cylinder sets:
$$
C = \pi_1^{-1}(\{H\}) \cap \pi_3^{-1}(\{T\}) \cap \pi_7^{-1}(\{H\}).
$$
This illustrates the fundamental idea of a cylinder set: A cylinder event specifies finitely many observations and ignores the rest.
:::

We now give the formal definition of the product $\sigma$-algebra for an arbitrary index set.

::: {#def-product-sigma-algebra-general}
## Product $\sigma$-Algebra for an Arbitrary Index Set
Let $J$ be an arbitrary index set and let $\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}$ be measurable spaces. Set $\Omega \triangleq \prod_{j \in J}\Omega_j$. The **product $\sigma$-algebra** is the $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ generated by the **cylinder sets**:
$$
\bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j \triangleq \sigma\left( \left\{ \pi_j^{-1}(B_j) \;\middle|\; j \in J,\ B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \right\} \right),
$$ {#eq-general-product-sigma}
equivalently the $\sigma$-algebra generated by those products $\prod_{j \in J} B_j$ with $B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j$ for every $j$ and $B_j = \Omega_j$ for all but finitely many $j$.
:::

* **Notation ($\sigma$-algebra generated by a family of maps):** Given maps $g_i : \Omega \to \Omega_i'$ into measurable spaces $(\Omega_i', \mathcal{F}_i')$, $i \in I$, define
$$
\sigma(\{g_i \mid i \in I\}) \triangleq \sigma\left( \bigcup_{i \in I} g_i^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_i') \right).
$$ {#eq-sigma-of-maps}
This is the **smallest** $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ making every $g_i$ measurable: a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ on $\Omega$ renders every $g_i$ measurable **iff** $g_i^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_i') \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ for all $i \in I$, iff $\mathcal{A} \supseteq \sigma(\{g_i \mid i \in I\})$. With this notation, @eq-general-product-sigma reads $\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\{\pi_j \mid j \in J\})$.

::: {#rem-uncountable-products}
## The Rectangle Definition Does Not Extend to Uncountable $J$
For **countable** $J$ the cylinder definition @eq-general-product-sigma agrees with the naive rectangle definition, because then
$$
\prod_{j \in J} B_j = \bigcap_{j \in J} \pi_j^{-1}(B_j)
$$
is a *countable* intersection of cylinders. For **uncountable** $J$ the two differ, and $\sigma\big(\{\prod_{j \in J}B_j\}\big)$ is strictly larger than $\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j$.
:::

:::{#lem-canonical-projections-measurable}
Let $J$ be an arbitrary index set and $\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}$ measurable spaces. Each canonical projection $\pi_k : \prod_{j \in J}\Omega_j \to \Omega_k$, $k \in J$, is $\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k$-measurable.
:::

:::{.proof}
## Proof of @lem-canonical-projections-measurable
To prove that $\pi_k$ is measurable, we must show that $\pi_k^{-1}(A)\in \bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j$ for every $A\in\mathcal{F}_k$. Take an arbitrary $A\in\mathcal{F}_k$. By @def-product-sigma-algebra-general, $\pi_k^{-1}(A)$ is one of the generating cylinder sets of $\bigotimes_{j \in J}\mathcal{F}_j$, hence lies in it.

In the finite case $J = \{1,\dots,d\}$ one can argue directly from @def-product-sigma-algebra. By the definition of $\pi_k$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_k^{-1}(A) &= \left\{\omega \in \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j \mid \pi_k(\omega) \in A \right\}= \left\{\omega \in \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j \mid \omega_k \in A \right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$
This set can be written as the rectangle
$$
\pi_k^{-1}(A) = \Omega_1 \times \dots \times \Omega_{k-1} \times A \times \Omega_{k+1} \times \dots \times \Omega_d.
$$
Since $\Omega_j \in \mathcal{F}_j$ for all $j \neq k$ and $A \in \mathcal{F}_k$, it follows that $\pi_k^{-1}(A) \in \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j$. Therefore, $\pi_k$ is measurable.
:::

The following lemma characterizes the product $\sigma$-algebra in terms of the canonical projections. It shows that the product $\sigma$-algebra is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j$ that makes all coordinate projections measurable.

:::{#lem-product-sigma-algebra}
Let $\{(\Omega_j,\mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j=1}^d$ be a finite family of measurable spaces and, for $k \in \{1, \dots, d\}$, let $\pi_k: \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j \to \Omega_k$ be defined by $\pi_k(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) = \omega_k$. Then 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j &= \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})\\
&=\sigma(\{\pi^{-1}_k(B_k) \mid 1 \le k \le d, B_k \in \mathcal{F}_k\}).
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

:::{.proof}
## Proof of @lem-product-sigma-algebra

Let $\mathcal{R} \triangleq \left\{ \prod_{j=1}^d B_j \;\middle|\; B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \text{ for } 1 \le j \le d \right\}$ denote the collection of product rectangles on $\Omega = \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j$. By @def-product-sigma-algebra, the product $\sigma$-algebra is $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\mathcal{R})$.

The second equality in the statement is @eq-sigma-of-maps applied to the family $\{\pi_k\}_{k=1}^d$, i.e. it holds by definition of $\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$; as recorded there, this is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ making every $\pi_k$ measurable. It therefore remains to prove the first equality, which we do by mutual inclusion between $\sigma(\mathcal{R})$ and $\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$.

1. **$(\subseteq)$ Inclusion:**
   Let $E \in \bigcup_{k=1}^d \pi_k^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_k)$. Then $E = \pi_k^{-1}(B_k)$ for some $k \in \{1, \dots, d\}$ and $B_k \in \mathcal{F}_k$.
   We can express $E$ as a product rectangle:
   $$
   E = \pi_k^{-1}(B_k) = \Omega_1 \times \dots \times \Omega_{k-1} \times B_k \times \Omega_{k+1} \times \dots \times \Omega_d
   $$
   Since $\Omega_j \in \mathcal{F}_j$ for all $j \neq k$ and $B_k \in \mathcal{F}_k$, it follows that $E \in \mathcal{R} \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{R})$. Thus, $\bigcup_{k=1}^d \pi_k^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_k) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{R})$. Since $\sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$ is generated by this collection, we conclude:
   $$
   \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\}) \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{R}) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j
   $$

2. **$(\supseteq)$ Inclusion:**
   Let $R = \prod_{j=1}^d B_j \in \mathcal{R}$ be an arbitrary product rectangle, where $B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j$ for each $j \in \{1, \dots, d\}$.
   Notice that $R$ can be written as a finite intersection of preimages under projection maps:
   $$
   R = \bigcap_{j=1}^d \pi_j^{-1}(B_j)
   $$
   Indeed, for any $(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) \in \prod_{j=1}^d \Omega_j$:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   &(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) \in \bigcap_{j=1}^d \pi_j^{-1}(B_j) \\
   &\iff \pi_j(\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) = \omega_j \in B_j \text{ for all } j \\
   &\iff (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d) \in \prod_{j=1}^d B_j = R.
   \end{aligned}
   $$ 
   For each $j$, $B_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \implies \pi_j^{-1}(B_j) \in \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$. Since a $\sigma$-algebra is closed under finite intersections, $R \in \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$.
   Thus, $\mathcal{R} \subseteq \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$, which implies:
   $$
   \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\mathcal{R}) \subseteq \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})
   $$

Combining both inclusions yields $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{F}_j = \sigma(\{\pi_k \mid 1 \le k \le d\})$, which together with the second equality noted above completes the proof.
:::

**Some Observations**:

- Consequently, for finite $J = \{1,\dots,d\}$ the rectangle definition @def-product-sigma-algebra and the cylinder definition @def-product-sigma-algebra-general agree, and the product $\sigma$-algebra is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\prod_{j=1}^d\Omega_j$ that makes all coordinate projections $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$ measurable.

* **Borel $\sigma$-Algebra Identity:** $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$.
  * *Proof.* $(\supseteq)$ Each projection $\pi_j : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, hence $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable; so $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ makes every $\pi_j$ measurable and therefore contains $\sigma(\{\pi_j \mid 1\le j\le d\}) = \bigotimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ by @lem-product-sigma-algebra. $(\subseteq)$ Every open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is a **countable** union of open boxes $\prod_{j=1}^d(a_j,b_j)$ with rational $a_j < b_j$, and each such box is a measurable rectangle; hence $U \in \bigotimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$. Since the open sets generate $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, we get $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d) \subseteq \bigotimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$.
  * *Caveat.* The inclusion $(\subseteq)$ uses **second countability** of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and does **not** hold for general topological spaces: if $X$ is a discrete space of cardinality $> \mathfrak{c}$, then $\mathcal{B}(X) = 2^X$, $X\times X$ is discrete so the diagonal $\Delta$ is Borel in $X \times X$, yet $\Delta \notin \mathcal{B}(X) \otimes \mathcal{B}(X)$. In general one only has $\mathcal{B}(X) \otimes \mathcal{B}(Y) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(X \times Y)$, with equality when $X$ and $Y$ are second countable.

---

## Product Measurability Lemma

The following lemma characterizes the measurability of functions into a product space in terms of the measurability of their component functions.

::: {#lem-product-measurability}
Let $\{(\Omega_j, \mathcal{F}_j)\}_{j \in J}$ and $(\Upsilon, \mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces. A function $f: \Upsilon \to \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j$-measurable if and only if the component mapping $\pi_k \circ f: \Upsilon \to \Omega_k$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k$-measurable for every $k \in J$.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @lem-product-measurability
Let $\Omega \triangleq \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j$ and let $\mathcal{F} \triangleq \bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j$ denote the product $\sigma$-algebra.

**$(\Rightarrow)$ Forward Direction:**  
Assume $f: \Upsilon \to \Omega$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}$-measurable.  
Fix any $k \in J$. By @lem-canonical-projections-measurable, the canonical projection map $\pi_k: \Omega \to \Omega_k$ is $\mathcal{F} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k$-measurable because $\pi_k^{-1}(E_k) \in \mathcal{F}$ for all $E_k \in \mathcal{F}_k$.  
Since the composition of two measurable maps is measurable, the component map $\pi_k \circ f: \Upsilon \to \Omega_k$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k$-measurable for every $k \in J$.

**$(\Leftarrow)$ Backward Direction:**  
Assume that $\pi_k \circ f: \Upsilon \to \Omega_k$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k$-measurable for every $k \in J$.  
Define the generating collection of cylinder sets on $\Omega$ by:
$$
\mathcal{G} \triangleq \bigcup_{j \in J} \pi_j^{-1}(\mathcal{F}_j) = \left\{ \pi_j^{-1}(E_j) \;\middle|\; j \in J,\, E_j \in \mathcal{F}_j \right\}
$$
By @def-product-sigma-algebra-general, $\mathcal{F} = \sigma(\mathcal{G})$. (For finite $J$ this is consistent with @def-product-sigma-algebra by @lem-product-sigma-algebra.)

To prove that $f$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}$-measurable, we must show that $f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{B}$ for all $E \in \mathcal{F}$. Consider the set of preimages under $f$:
$$
\mathcal{A} \triangleq \{ E \subseteq \Omega \mid f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{B} \}
$$
Then $\mathcal{A}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$, since preimages commute with complements and countable unions: $f^{-1}(\Omega) = \Upsilon \in \mathcal{B}$, $f^{-1}(E^c) = (f^{-1}(E))^c$, and $f^{-1}(\bigcup_n E_n) = \bigcup_n f^{-1}(E_n)$.

Now, take any generating set $A \in \mathcal{G}$. Then $A = \pi_j^{-1}(E_j)$ for some $j \in J$ and $E_j \in \mathcal{F}_j$. Evaluating the preimage under $f$ gives:
$$
f^{-1}(A) = f^{-1}\left( \pi_j^{-1}(E_j) \right) = (\pi_j \circ f)^{-1}(E_j)
$$
By hypothesis, $\pi_j \circ f$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_j$-measurable, so $(\pi_j \circ f)^{-1}(E_j) \in \mathcal{B}$. Thus, $A \in \mathcal{A}$, which implies $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{A}$.

Since $\mathcal{A}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra containing $\mathcal{G}$, it contains the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\mathcal{G}$:
$$
\mathcal{F} = \sigma(\mathcal{G}) \subseteq \mathcal{A}
$$
Hence, $f^{-1}(E) \in \mathcal{B}$ for all $E \in \mathcal{F}$, proving that $f$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}$-measurable.
:::

**Some Observations**:

- **This lemma is often written more simply as**: writing $f_k \triangleq \pi_k \circ f : \Upsilon \to \Omega_k$ for the $k$-th **component map** of $f$, the map $f: \Upsilon \to \prod_{j \in J} \Omega_j$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \bigotimes_{j \in J} \mathcal{F}_j$-measurable if and only if each component map $f_k$ is $\mathcal{B} \,/\, \mathcal{F}_k$-measurable for all $k \in J$.

---

## Tensor Product Functions

Given $f_1: \Omega_1 \to \mathbb{R}$ and $f_2: \Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}$, their **tensor product** $f_1 \otimes f_2: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by:
$$
(f_1 \otimes f_2)(\omega_1, \omega_2) \triangleq f_1(\omega_1) \cdot f_2(\omega_2)
$$ {#eq-tensor-product-def}

::: {#lem-tensor-product-measurable}
Let $f_i : \Omega_i \to \mathbb{R}$ be $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable for $i = 1,2$. Then $f_1 \otimes f_2$ is $(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable.
:::

:::{.proof}
## Proof of @lem-tensor-product-measurable
Note first that $f_1 \otimes f_2 = (f_1 \circ \pi_1) \cdot (f_2 \circ \pi_2)$.

- By @lem-canonical-projections-measurable the coordinate projections $\pi_i$ are $(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)/\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable; since $f_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable and compositions of measurable maps are measurable, $f_1\circ\pi_1$ and $f_2\circ\pi_2$ are $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable real-valued functions.
- By @lem-product-measurability, the pair map
$$
\Phi \triangleq (f_1\circ\pi_1,\, f_2\circ\pi_2) : \Omega_1\times\Omega_2 \to \mathbb{R}^2
$$
is $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2) \,/\, \big(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\big)$-measurable, since both of its components are measurable. By the Borel $\sigma$-algebra identity $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)$, $\Phi$ is in fact $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)$-measurable. (This step is exactly where second countability of $\mathbb{R}$ is used.)
- The multiplication map $m:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, $m(x,y)=xy$, is continuous and hence $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^2)/\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable. Therefore
$$ 
f_1\otimes f_2 = m\circ\Phi
$$
is $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable.
:::

---

## Iterated Integrals for Non-Negative Functions

The following theorem is the **iterated-integral form of Tonelli's theorem**. It establishes the measurability of slice functions and the equality of iterated integrals for **non-negative** measurable functions on product spaces. It is logically prior to the product measure itself: it is what makes @cor-product-measure-existence possible. The form of Tonelli's theorem that also identifies these iterated integrals with the integral against $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ is @thm-tonelli in Lecture 14.3.

::: {#thm-iterated-integrals}
## Tonelli's Theorem (Iterated-Integral Form)
Let $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2)$ be measurable spaces and let $f: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to [0, \infty]$ be a non-negative $(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable function. Then:

1. **Slice Measurability** (no hypothesis on the measures is required):
   * For every fixed $\omega_2 \in \Omega_2$, the slice function $\omega_1 \mapsto f(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable.
   * For every fixed $\omega_1 \in \Omega_1$, the slice function $\omega_2 \mapsto f(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable.

Assume in addition that $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are measures on $(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)$ that are **$\sigma$-finite**. Then:

2. **Integrated Slice Measurability:**
   * The function $\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable (as a map into $([0,\infty],\mathcal{B}([0,\infty]))$).
   * The function $\omega_2 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_1} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1)$ is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable.
3. **Equality of Iterated Integrals** (both sides being elements of $[0,\infty]$):
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   &\int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \right) \mu_1(d\omega_1) \\
   &= \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) \right) \mu_2(d\omega_2)
   \end{aligned}
   $$ {#eq-iterated-integrals-equality}
:::

::: {#rem-sigma-finiteness-necessary}
## $\sigma$-Finiteness Is Necessary in Parts 2 and 3
Let $\Omega_1 = \Omega_2 = [0,1]$ with $\mathcal{F}_1 = \mathcal{F}_2 = \mathcal{B}([0,1])$, let $\mu_1 = \lambda$ be Lebesgue measure and let $\mu_2$ be **counting measure** (which is not $\sigma$-finite on $[0,1]$). The diagonal
$$
D \triangleq \{(x,x) \mid x \in [0,1]\}
$$
is closed in $[0,1]^2$, hence $D \in \mathcal{B}([0,1]^2) = \mathcal{B}([0,1])\otimes\mathcal{B}([0,1])$, so $f = \mathbf{1}_D$ is product-measurable and non-negative:
$$
f(x,y)=\mathbf{1}_D(x,y) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } x=y,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega_1}\!\!\int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2\, d\mu_1 &= \int_{\Omega_1}\left(\int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{\{x\}}(y)\mu_2(dy)\right) d\mu_1\\
&=\int_{\Omega_1}\mu_2(\{x\}) d\mu_1\\
&=\int_{[0,1]} 1 \, \lambda(dx) = 1,
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega_2}\!\!\int_{\Omega_1} f \, d\mu_1\, d\mu_2 &= \int_{\Omega_2}\left(\int_{\Omega_1} \mathbf{1}_{\{y\}}(x)\mu_1(dx) \right) \mu_2(dy)\\
&=\int_{[0,1]} 0 \, \mu_2(dy) = 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus @eq-iterated-integrals-equality fails. Note that part 1 still holds here, as it must. The same example shows that uniqueness in @cor-product-measure-existence fails without $\sigma$-finiteness.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @thm-iterated-integrals

Steps 1–3 prove all three assertions under the temporary hypothesis
$$
\mu_1(\Omega_1) < \infty \quad\text{and}\quad \mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty,
$$
which is assumed throughout Steps 1–3. Step 4 removes it: it derives part 1 with no hypothesis on the measures at all, and parts 2–3 under $\sigma$-finiteness.

### Step 1: Verification for Elementary Tensor Products

Let $f = f_1 \otimes f_2$, where $f_1 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mathbb{R})$ and $f_2 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R})$, i.e. $f_i$ is bounded, real-valued and $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable. By @lem-tensor-product-measurable, $f$ is $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable, and it is bounded, so $f \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R})$. Since $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are finite and $f_1,f_2$ are bounded, all integrals appearing below are finite real numbers, so no $\infty - \infty$ or $0\cdot\infty$ ambiguity can arise.

1. **Slice Measurability:** For fixed $\omega_2 \in \Omega_2$, $\omega_1 \mapsto (f_1 \otimes f_2)(\omega_1, \omega_2) = f_2(\omega_2) \cdot f_1(\omega_1)$ is a constant multiple of an $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable function, hence $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable. By symmetry, $\omega_2 \mapsto f_1(\omega_1) f_2(\omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable for fixed $\omega_1$.
2. **Integrated Slice Functions:** Fix $\omega_1 \in \Omega_1$. Since $f_2$ is bounded and $\mu_2(\Omega_2)<\infty$, $f_2 \in L^1(\mu_2)$ and $\int_{\Omega_2} f_2\,d\mu_2 \in \mathbb{R}$; since $f_1(\omega_1) \in \mathbb{R}$ is a finite constant, it may be pulled out of the integral:
   $$
   I_2(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} f_1(\omega_1) f_2(\omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) = f_1(\omega_1) \int_{\Omega_2} f_2 \, d\mu_2
   $$
   As $\int_{\Omega_2} f_2 \, d\mu_2$ is a finite constant, $I_2$ is a constant multiple of $f_1$ and hence $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable (and bounded).
3. **Equality of Iterated Integrals:** $I_2$ is bounded and $\mu_1(\Omega_1)<\infty$, so $I_2 \in L^1(\mu_1)$ and integrating over $\Omega_1$ gives:
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_1} I_2(\omega_1) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) = \left( \int_{\Omega_1} f_1 \, d\mu_1 \right) \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f_2 \, d\mu_2 \right)
   $$
   Reversing the roles of the two coordinates in items 2 and 3 yields the same product of finite numbers for the other iterated integral, establishing equality.

---

### Step 2: Extension to Bounded Measurable Functions via Dynkin's Theorem

Define the space of test functions $\mathbb{M} \triangleq \{ f_1 \otimes f_2 \mid f_1 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mathbb{R}),\, f_2 \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R}) \}$.

* **$\mathbb{M}$ is a Multiplicative System:** For $f_1 \otimes f_2, g_1 \otimes g_2 \in \mathbb{M}$, $(f_1 \otimes f_2) \cdot (g_1 \otimes g_2) = (f_1 g_1) \otimes (f_2 g_2) \in \mathbb{M}$ because products of bounded measurable functions remain bounded and measurable.
* **$\mathbb{M}$ Generates $\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$:** We check both inclusions.
  * $(\supseteq)$ For $A_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1$ and $A_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2$, $\mathbf{1}_{A_1 \times A_2} = \mathbf{1}_{A_1} \otimes \mathbf{1}_{A_2} \in \mathbb{M}$, so $A_1\times A_2 = (\mathbf{1}_{A_1}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{A_2})^{-1}(\{1\}) \in \sigma(\mathbb{M})$. Since $\sigma(\mathbb{M})$ contains all measurable rectangles, $\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2 \subseteq \sigma(\mathbb{M})$.
  * $(\subseteq)$ By @lem-tensor-product-measurable every element of $\mathbb{M}$ is $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable, so $\sigma(\mathbb{M}) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2$.
  
  Hence $\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$.

Define $\mathbb{H} \subseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R})$ as the collection of bounded measurable functions $g$ satisfying:

1. For **every** fixed $\omega_2 \in \Omega_2$ the map $\omega_1 \mapsto g(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable, and for **every** fixed $\omega_1 \in \Omega_1$ the map $\omega_2 \mapsto g(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable.
2. The map $\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable and the map $\omega_2 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_1} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_1$ is $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable. (These integrals are well defined by property (1), and are finite real numbers because $g$ is bounded and $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are finite.)
3. $\int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1 = \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_1 \right) d\mu_2$.

**$\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}$:** By Step 1, every $f \in \mathbb{M}$ satisfies properties (1), (2), (3) above, so $\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}$.

We verify the remaining properties of $\mathbb{H}$:

1. **Vector Space containing $1$:** Let $g, \tilde{g} \in \mathbb{H}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Property (1) for $a g + b\tilde g$ is immediate. For (2) and (3), note that all four functions $g(\cdot,\omega_2)$, $g(\omega_1,\cdot)$, $\tilde g(\cdot,\omega_2)$, $\tilde g(\omega_1,\cdot)$ are bounded and $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are **finite**, so every integral involved is a finite real number and linearity of the integral applies without any $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity; consequently
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_2}(a g + b\tilde g)(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2 = a\!\int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2 + b\!\int_{\Omega_2} \tilde g(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2,
   $$
   which is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable, and the two iterated integrals of $ag+b\tilde g$ agree because they do for $g$ and for $\tilde g$. Hence $\mathbb{H}$ is a vector space. Since $1 = 1 \otimes 1 \in \mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}$, the constant function $1$ belongs to $\mathbb{H}$.
2. **Closed under Bounded Convergence:** Let $\{g_n\} \subset \mathbb{H}$ with $|g_n(\omega_1, \omega_2)| \le M < \infty$ for all $n$ and all $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$, and $g_n \to g$ pointwise on $\Omega_1\times\Omega_2$. Then $g$ is $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable and $|g|\le M$, so $g \in \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2,\mathbb{R})$.

   * *Slice Limits:* For fixed $\omega_2$, $g_n(\cdot,\omega_2) \to g(\cdot,\omega_2)$ pointwise, and each $g_n(\cdot,\omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable by property (1) for $g_n$; a pointwise limit of measurable functions is measurable, so $g$ satisfies property (1) (and symmetrically in the other coordinate).
   * *Slice Integrals:* Define $h_n(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} g_n(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2)$. Fix $\omega_1$. Since $|g_n(\omega_1,\cdot)| \le M$ and $\mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty$, the constant $M$ is $\mu_2$-integrable and dominates the sequence. By the Dominated Convergence Theorem (DCT):
     $$
     \lim_{n \to \infty} h_n(\omega_1) = \int_{\Omega_2} g(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \triangleq h(\omega_1)
     $$
     Since each $h_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable by property (2) for $g_n$, their pointwise limit $h$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable, verifying property (2) for $g$ (and symmetrically in the other coordinate).
   * *Iterated Integral Limit:* Note that $|h_n(\omega_1)| \le M \mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty$ for all $n$ and $\omega_1$, and $\mu_1(\Omega_1)<\infty$, so the constant $M\mu_2(\Omega_2)$ is $\mu_1$-integrable and dominates $\{h_n\}$. Applying DCT a second time with respect to $\mu_1$:
     $$
     \int_{\Omega_1} h(\omega_1) \, d\mu_1 = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\Omega_1} h_n(\omega_1) \, d\mu_1
     $$
     By symmetry, the analogous limit holds for the reversed order of integration. Since the two iterated integrals agree for each $g_n$ by property (3), and both sides converge, they agree for $g$, verifying property (3).

All hypotheses of Dynkin's Multiplicative Systems Theorem (@thm-dynkin-multiplicative-system) are satisfied: $\mathbb{M}$ is a multiplicative system, $\mathbb{M} \subseteq \mathbb{H}$, $\mathbb{H}$ is a vector space of bounded functions containing $1$ that is closed under bounded convergence, and $\sigma(\mathbb{M}) = \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$. Therefore
$$
\mathbb{H} \supseteq \mathbb{B}(\Omega_1 \times \Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2, \mathbb{R}),
$$
i.e. **every** bounded $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable function satisfies (1), (2), (3).

---

### Step 3: Extension to Non-Negative Functions

Let $f: \Omega_1 \times \Omega_2 \to [0, \infty]$ be non-negative and $(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable.

1. **Truncation Sequence:** Define $f_n \triangleq \min\{f, n\}$. Since $f$ is $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable as a map into $[0,\infty]$ and $x \mapsto \min\{x,n\}$ is Borel, $f_n$ is non-negative, bounded and $(\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable, hence real-valued and in $\mathbb{B}(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2,\mathbb{R})$. By the conclusion of Step 2, $f_n \in \mathbb{H}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $f_n \uparrow f$ pointwise.
2. **Slice Measurability:** For fixed $\omega_2$, $f_n(\cdot, \omega_2) \uparrow f(\cdot, \omega_2)$ pointwise, and each $f_n(\cdot,\omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable by property (1) of $\mathbb{H}$. As a pointwise limit of measurable functions, $\omega_1 \mapsto f(\omega_1, \omega_2)$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable (as a map into $[0,\infty]$). Symmetrically for the other coordinate.
3. **Monotone Convergence Theorem:** Fix $\omega_1$. Since $0 \le f_n(\omega_1,\cdot) \uparrow f(\omega_1,\cdot)$, MCT on $\Omega_2$ gives:
   $$
   I_{2, n}(\omega_1) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_2} f_n(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \triangleq I_2(\omega_1)
   $$
   Since each $I_{2, n}$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable by property (2) of $\mathbb{H}$, the pointwise limit $I_2$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable (possibly $[0,\infty]$-valued). Symmetrically for the other order.
4. **Iterated Integrals:** Since $0 \le I_{2,n} \uparrow I_2$, applying MCT a second time on $\Omega_1$:
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f_n \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1
   $$
   and symmetrically for the reversed order. Since the two iterated integrals agree for each $f_n$ by property (3) of $\mathbb{H}$, and both sides converge in $[0,\infty]$, taking $n \to \infty$ establishes equality of the iterated integrals for $f$.

---

### Step 4: Extension to $\sigma$-finite Measures

The preceding three steps establish the theorem under $\mu_1(\Omega_1) < \infty$ and $\mu_2(\Omega_2) < \infty$. We now extend to the general $\sigma$-finite case.

Since $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are $\sigma$-finite, choose **increasing** sequences $A_k \nearrow \Omega_1$ in $\mathcal{F}_1$ and $B_k \nearrow \Omega_2$ in $\mathcal{F}_2$ with $\mu_1(A_k) < \infty$ and $\mu_2(B_k) < \infty$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$. (If $\Omega_i = \bigcup_m C^{(i)}_m$ with $\mu_i(C^{(i)}_m)<\infty$, replace $C^{(i)}_m$ by $\bigcup_{l \le m} C^{(i)}_l$, which is still of finite measure by finite subadditivity.)

Rather than passing to trace $\sigma$-algebras on $A_k$ and $B_k$, we truncate the **measures** on the original spaces. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define
$$
\mu_1^{(k)}(E) \triangleq \mu_1(E \cap A_k) \ \ (E \in \mathcal{F}_1), \qquad
\mu_2^{(k)}(F) \triangleq \mu_2(F \cap B_k) \ \ (F \in \mathcal{F}_2).
$$
These are measures on $(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)$ (countable additivity is inherited from $\mu_i$), and they are **finite**: $\mu_1^{(k)}(\Omega_1) = \mu_1(A_k) < \infty$ and $\mu_2^{(k)}(\Omega_2) = \mu_2(B_k) < \infty$. Moreover, for every non-negative $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable $g_1$ and every non-negative $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable $g_2$,
$$
\int_{\Omega_1} g_1 \, d\mu_1^{(k)} = \int_{\Omega_1} g_1 \, \mathbf{1}_{A_k} \, d\mu_1, \qquad \int_{\Omega_2} g_2 \, d\mu_2^{(k)} = \int_{\Omega_2} g_2 \, \mathbf{1}_{B_k} \, d\mu_2,
$$ {#eq-truncated-measure-integral}
which holds for indicators by definition of $\mu_i^{(k)}$, extends to non-negative simple functions by linearity, and to all non-negative measurable functions by MCT.

1. **Part 1 needs no assumption on the measures.** Apply Steps 1–3 with the (finite) **zero measures** $\mu_1 \equiv 0$ and $\mu_2 \equiv 0$ on $(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)$: properties (2) and (3) in the definition of $\mathbb{H}$ then hold trivially, while property (1) does not involve the measures at all. Steps 1–3 therefore yield that every non-negative $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable $f$ has $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable and $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable slices, for arbitrary measurable spaces $(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1)$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2)$. This proves part 1 of the theorem in full generality.

2. **Finite-measure case applies to the truncated measures.** Fix $k$ and let $f \ge 0$ be $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable. Applying Steps 1–3 to the finite measure spaces $(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1,\mu_1^{(k)})$ and $(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2,\mu_2^{(k)})$ and to $f$ itself gives that
   $$
   \omega_1 \longmapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\, \mu_2^{(k)}(d\omega_2) = \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\,\mathbf{1}_{B_k}(\omega_2)\, \mu_2(d\omega_2)
   $$
   (the equality being @eq-truncated-measure-integral) is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable on **all** of $\Omega_1$, and that
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_1}\!\!\int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2^{(k)} \, d\mu_1^{(k)} = \int_{\Omega_2}\!\!\int_{\Omega_1} f \, d\mu_1^{(k)} \, d\mu_2^{(k)}.
   $$
   Using @eq-truncated-measure-integral twice on each side, and writing $f_k \triangleq f \cdot \mathbf{1}_{A_k \times B_k}$ (so that $f\,\mathbf{1}_{B_k}(\omega_2)\,\mathbf{1}_{A_k}(\omega_1) = f_k$), this reads
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} f_k \, d\mu_2 \, d\mu_1 = \int_{\Omega_2} \int_{\Omega_1} f_k \, d\mu_1 \, d\mu_2,
   $$
   and $\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f_k(\omega_1,\omega_2)\,d\mu_2 = \mathbf{1}_{A_k}(\omega_1)\int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\mathbf{1}_{B_k}(\omega_2)\,d\mu_2$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable.

3. **Monotone limit recovers $f$:** Because $A_k$ and $B_k$ are increasing, $A_k \times B_k \nearrow \Omega_1\times\Omega_2$, so the **single-indexed** sequence $f_k = f\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A_k\times B_k}$ satisfies $0 \le f_k \uparrow f$ pointwise. By MCT applied to the inner integral, for every $\omega_1$,
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_2} f_k(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2.
   $$
   Hence $\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2$ is $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable as the pointwise limit of the $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable functions from item 2, proving part 2 (symmetrically in the other coordinate).

4. **Equality of iterated integrals:** By item 3 the inner integrals increase, $\int_{\Omega_2} f_k(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_2} f(\omega_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_2$ for every $\omega_1$, so MCT applied to the outer integral gives
   $$
   \int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} f_{k} \, d\mu_2 \, d\mu_1 \uparrow \int_{\Omega_1} \int_{\Omega_2} f \, d\mu_2 \, d\mu_1,
   $$
   and by symmetry the same limit holds for the reversed order. Since the two sides are equal at each stage $k$ by item 2, and both converge in $[0,\infty]$, they are equal in the limit. This proves part 3 and completes the proof.
:::



## Construction and Uniqueness of Product Measure

::: {#cor-product-measure-existence}
## Existence and Uniqueness of the Product Measure
Let $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{F}_1, \mu_1)$ and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{F}_2, \mu_2)$ be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces.

1. **Existence and uniqueness.** There exists exactly one measure $\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2$ on $\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$ satisfying
$$
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_1 \times E_2) = \mu_1(E_1)\, \mu_2(E_2),
$$ {#eq-product-measure-rectangles}
for all $E_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1,\ E_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2$ with the convention $0\cdot\infty = 0$. Moreover $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ is $\sigma$-finite.

2. **Representation by iterated integrals.** For every $E \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) &= \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_2(d\omega_2) \right) \mu_1(d\omega_1) \\
&= \int_{\Omega_2} \left( \int_{\Omega_1} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, \mu_1(d\omega_1) \right) \mu_2(d\omega_2).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-product-measure-iterated}
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @cor-product-measure-existence
For every $E \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$ the function $\mathbf{1}_E$ is non-negative and $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable, so by @thm-iterated-integrals (parts 1 and 2) the inner integral $\omega_1 \mapsto \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2)\,d\mu_2$ is well defined for every $\omega_1$ and $\mathcal{F}_1$-measurable. Hence the following definition is well-posed. Define:
$$
(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) \triangleq \int_{\Omega_1} \left( \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \right) d\mu_1.
$$

1. **Non-negativity and empty set:** Since $\mathbf{1}_E \ge 0$, we have $(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) \ge 0$. Setting $E = \emptyset$ gives $\mathbf{1}_\emptyset = 0$, so $(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(\emptyset) = 0$.
2. **Countable Additivity:** Let $E = \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k$ with **pairwise disjoint** $E_k \in \mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$. Disjointness gives $\mathbf{1}_E = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{E_k}$ pointwise, and the partial sums $S_N \triangleq \sum_{k \le N}\mathbf{1}_{E_k}$ satisfy $0 \le S_N \uparrow \mathbf{1}_E$. Fix $\omega_1$; by MCT on $\Omega_2$ together with finite additivity of the integral,
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_E(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 &= \lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{N} \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{E_k}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 \\
   &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{E_k}(\omega_1, \omega_2) \, d\mu_2 .
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   The partial sums of the right-hand side increase in $N$, so applying MCT again on $\Omega_1$ (and finite additivity there) gives $(\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty (\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_k)$. Hence $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ is a measure on $\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2$.
3. **Rectangle Value:** For $E = E_1 \times E_2$ we have $\mathbf{1}_{E_1\times E_2}(\omega_1,\omega_2) = \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1)\mathbf{1}_{E_2}(\omega_2)$, so the inner integral evaluates as $\int_{\Omega_2} \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1)\mathbf{1}_{E_2}(\omega_2)\,d\mu_2 = \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1)\,\mu_2(E_2)$ (with $0\cdot\infty = 0$ when $\omega_1 \notin E_1$ and $\mu_2(E_2)=\infty$). Integrating over $\Omega_1$:
   $$
   (\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_1 \times E_2) = \int_{\Omega_1} \mathbf{1}_{E_1}(\omega_1) \mu_2(E_2) \, d\mu_1 = \mu_1(E_1) \mu_2(E_2),
   $$
   which is @eq-product-measure-rectangles. The equality of the two iterated integrals in @eq-product-measure-iterated is @thm-iterated-integrals part 3 applied to $f = \mathbf{1}_E$, which is non-negative and $(\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2)$-measurable.
4. **$\sigma$-finiteness of $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ and uniqueness:** The collection
   $$
   \mathcal{P} \triangleq \{E_1 \times E_2 \mid E_1 \in \mathcal{F}_1,\, E_2 \in \mathcal{F}_2\}
   $$
   is a $\pi$-system, since $(E_1 \times E_2) \cap (F_1 \times F_2) = (E_1 \cap F_1) \times (E_2 \cap F_2) \in \mathcal{P}$, and $\sigma(\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2$ by @def-product-sigma-algebra.

   By $\sigma$-finiteness we may choose **increasing** sequences $A_m \nearrow \Omega_1$ and $B_m \nearrow \Omega_2$ with $\mu_1(A_m)<\infty$ and $\mu_2(B_m)<\infty$ (replace a given countable cover by the unions of its initial segments). Put
   $$
   S_m \triangleq A_m \times B_m \in \mathcal{P}.
   $$
   Then $S_m \nearrow \Omega_1\times\Omega_2$ and, by item 3, $(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(S_m) = \mu_1(A_m)\mu_2(B_m) < \infty$; in particular $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ is $\sigma$-finite.

   Now let $\nu$ be any measure on $\mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2$ satisfying @eq-product-measure-rectangles. Then $\nu$ agrees with $\mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ on $\mathcal{P}$, and $\nu(S_m) = \mu_1(A_m)\mu_2(B_m) < \infty$ with $S_m \in \mathcal{P}$, $S_m \nearrow \Omega_1\times\Omega_2$. By the uniqueness theorem for measures (Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem applied to $\mathcal{L}_m \triangleq \{E \in \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2 \mid \nu(E\cap S_m) = (\mu_1\otimes\mu_2)(E \cap S_m)\}$, which is a $\lambda$-system containing $\mathcal{P}$, followed by continuity from below as $m \to \infty$), $\nu = \mu_1\otimes\mu_2$ on $\sigma(\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{F}_1\otimes\mathcal{F}_2$. See also @lem-pi-system-uniqueness.
:::


---


## Takeaways

1. The product $\sigma$-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles in finite products and by finite-coordinate cylinder sets in arbitrary products. It is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra making all coordinate projections measurable.
2. In an uncountable product, product-measurable sets depend on at most countably many coordinates; unrestricted products need not be product measurable. This is why the definition uses cylinders.
3. A map into a product space is measurable exactly when each of its coordinate maps is measurable. In particular, tensor products of measurable functions are measurable on the product space.
4. For a product-measurable set or non-negative product-measurable function, its coordinate sections are measurable. Under $\sigma$-finite measures, integrating a non-negative function over either coordinate produces a measurable function, and the two iterated integrals agree.
5. The product measure $\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2$ is the unique $\sigma$-finite measure on $\mathcal{F}_1 \otimes \mathcal{F}_2$ satisfying
   $$
   (\mu_1 \otimes \mu_2)(E_1 \times E_2) = \mu_1(E_1)\mu_2(E_2).
   $$
   It can equivalently be computed by integrating the indicator of a measurable set in either order.
